title: Self-Rising Flour: What It Is and How It Differs From All-Purpose Flour With Leavener

seo.title: Self-Rising Flour: What It Is and How to Substitute It
seo.meta_description: Self-rising flour already contains baking powder and salt. Many versions also use softer lower-protein wheat than all-purpose flour. You can imitate it with flour, baking powder, and salt.
seo.search_intent: Understand what self-rising flour contains, how it differs from all-purpose flour, why protein matters, and how to substitute it correctly in recipes.

excerpt: Self-rising flour is a blend of flour, baking powder, and salt. Some brands also use softer wheat with less protein than standard all-purpose flour, so swapping between them changes not only leavening but also tenderness and liquid absorption.
content_html:
Self-rising flour is flour that already contains baking powder and a small amount of salt. Its purpose is to simplify recipes such as biscuits, scones, pancakes, and selected cakes by removing two ingredients you would otherwise measure separately.

But the difference often goes farther: traditional self-rising flours are frequently milled from softer wheat and contain less protein than standard all-purpose flour.

What exactly is in self-rising flour?

King Arthur defines self-rising flour as flour blended with baking powder and salt. Its product is made from soft wheat and contains about 8.5% protein, compared with roughly 11.7% in its all-purpose flour.

Other brands can use different percentages, so the label matters when texture is especially important.

Why does lower protein create more tender baking?

Wheat proteins form gluten after hydration and mixing. Lower-protein flour has less potential to create a strong elastic network.

That is useful for biscuits, cakes, pancakes, and scones, where a soft fragile crumb is preferable to bread-like chew.

It is not all-purpose flour plus baker's yeast

The word “rising” can create confusion. Self-rising flour contains chemical leavener — baking powder — not biological baker's yeast.

It does not need fermentation. Gas is generated by chemical reactions after the batter or dough is hydrated and heated.

How do you make a homemade version?

King Arthur suggests combining 1 cup/120 g all-purpose flour with 1½ teaspoons baking powder and ¼ teaspoon table salt.

This reproduces the leavening and salt system, but it does not transform an 11–12% protein flour into an 8–9% soft flour. The finished baked good may therefore be slightly less tender.

How do you substitute self-rising for all-purpose?

If a recipe already includes baking powder, self-rising flour can often replace the flour while the equivalent baking powder and salt are removed from the formula.

King Arthur recommends this most readily for recipes using roughly ½–1 teaspoon baking powder per cup of flour.

What if the recipe contains baking soda?

Do not automatically omit the soda. It serves a different purpose, reacting with acidic ingredients and also affecting color and flavor.

A formula can use self-rising flour and baking soda together when it needs to neutralize buttermilk, yogurt, molasses, or another acidic ingredient.

Self-rising flour is not a good bread-flour substitute

Bread flour has much more protein and is designed to build strong gluten. Self-rising flour goes in the opposite direction by prioritizing tenderness.

Using it in a yeast bread can weaken structure while also adding chemical leavener the formula was not designed for.

Why might liquid need adjustment?

Lower-protein flour can absorb liquid differently. King Arthur notes that switching between self-rising and all-purpose may require a small liquid adjustment.

Instead of adding every drop of milk immediately, hold back a small amount and correct consistency at the end.

The built-in leavener ages too

Because baking powder is already mixed into the flour, a very old bag can lose lifting power even if the flour itself does not smell spoiled. That is an important difference from plain flour.

The practical rule: self-rising flour equals flour plus baking powder plus salt, often with relatively low protein. A homemade blend reproduces the leavener, but flour strength still influences the final texture.

As always, the specific label matters when formulations differ. One name can cover products with different ingredients, salt levels, seaweed content, leavener, or flour protein. For predictable cooking, check the formulation and adjust the recipe to the product you actually have.

faq.question: What is in self-rising flour?
faq.answer: Flour, baking powder, and a small amount of salt; many brands also use relatively low-protein soft wheat.

faq.question: How can I make self-rising flour at home?
faq.answer: King Arthur's reference is 120 g all-purpose flour plus 1½ teaspoons baking powder and ¼ teaspoon salt.

faq.question: Is it flour with baker's yeast?
faq.answer: No. Self-rising flour uses chemical leavener, not biological yeast.
